reading_rules.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

An earlier inner-being observation with a node on the occurrences of a 3.1 row (any stage but lexical, layer-1, layer-2 and layer-3) is shown in the pull for information and may be actioned in `existing`: accepted, modified, deleted, merged or left, each with its reason, through observationrecord (RW-01, RW-09); nothing is demanded of it, and it counts for nothing in the check. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason. Every older live observation with a node on an occurrence of the row is answered in fill.older at the record of the row (RW-13); this rule's `existing` actions of stage 4 are unchanged.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.

Read outward from the verse, not inward from the scope's question. First record everything the verse carries, each with where it bears (chapter, thread, signpost); answer the scope's question last. A verse often has two or three significances, and none is dropped.
Read the verse in its passage and genre; name the speaker; explore figures for what they say about the inner being; take paired and opposite acts together. Restating a verse is not reading it.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.
Record how the M-code words work together (a relational observation). Record any pointer outside the verse separately, without resolving it inline.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route). A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Read the T3 operations, movement and force, negators (a refusal is an act), connectives, body parts, places, objects and nature for what they carry here; read every row, untagged ones too.

For every word that names an inner or bodily act, look at the original: the root's range in all three meaning sources read together, never one picked and the others dropped; the ESV renderings across its verses; whether the English adds or hides; the literal sense beside the rendering. Where more than one reading is open, record each, and mark the choice 'I read'.

Record each relevant word's face as it appears HERE: the circumstance in this verse and where the sense departs from the general gloss. Identifying and clarifying the face is lexical work; what the faces do for the inner being, and a double meaning in different scenarios, are layer 2 of the collection reading (layer-aspects-are-ledgered-and-never-left-open).
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
A literary or structural pattern is not an inner-being observation: log it as an open question instead. A human/divine comparison is recorded only where the text's own wording anchors it.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.
Morph is read, not carried: where occurrences of a word show different stems or voices, record whether the subject does, undergoes or causes the act.
A difference, or a specific inference, is its own observation, never folded into another.

A word that is only a homonym or a name, with no meaningful context, is recorded as such (tag no-human-context) and left. Data errors found while reading are flagged (tag data-error), not fixed in the reading.
The question catalogue's questions are prompts for the areas to explore. A question that does not apply is not answered, and no answer is manufactured beyond what the verse shows.
Faculty (heart, soul, spirit, mind) is reflected on at the end, over the scope, not per word.
Before reading the whole scope, read a few verses and have them checked.
No observation is changed except by a reading, and every change is recorded with its reason. An observation no longer supported by the verse is soft-deleted, with the reason.

A reading records findings of eight kinds (cfg_setting reading.observation_parts; the kind is the tag): face, qualification, party, statement, link, use, term, silence. A finding holds its text, meaning, implication, basis, its structured parts (ib_observation.parts: item, and mode, polarity, flag_type or grounds where its item needs them; reading.observation_items) and, on a party or link finding, its route; its nodes hold the verse, the word, the occurrence, the collection and its subgroup, the word's role in the finding and the reading that applied it. The silence kind is not used by Analysis_phase_1: a surface with no inner-being role is not recorded.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.
An observation about a word can be answered only by consulting this occurrence's verse, span and morph.
Verse references are resolved fresh at write time, never taken from the text written. Relations are recorded only on evidence.

A flag raised in reading (needs adjacent context, a pointer) states its reason and what the follow-up must establish, and is carried to an open item, not resolved inline. Can't-resolve is recorded, never guessed (tag could-not-resolve).
Where the evidence points to more than one reading, each is its own observation with its own evidence.
A re-read includes the observations already recorded for the verse, so the reading sees prior findings and builds on them.
Where a verse ends up for a finding is recorded on the node (ib_node.disposition, cfg_enum observation_disposition: told, claim, held, data, context, withdrawn), with its reason or carrier.
Missing data in the base extract is named as a gap, never substituted from memory or outside knowledge.

After recording, every observation is read back against the verse for sense. An uncertain one is recorded as uncertain (tag could-not-resolve, or basis read: 'I read'), never asserted. A rule found to be systematically wrong is raised as a config change with the learning, never worked round in the reading.

A word is read per its lettered Strong's code (its grain), never the bare lemma (B:113). The occurrences of a word with several senses are related per grain and never aggregated across grains: related verses are same-grain occurrences.

Content words carry the inner-being impact and are read even when no cluster tags them. Function words (particles, prepositions, conjunctions, suffixes, pronouns) get no observation of their own, except negators and connectives, which are read for what they do (RG-07). A T2 word never stands alone: it is read as the qualifier of what it binds to.

The words in cfg_setting reading.non_characteristic_strongs are never a verse's characteristic: superscription metadata and named external adversaries. They are read as standalone or as qualifiers. The list is per word, not per cluster, because a cluster can hold both kinds.

A tagged word that works adverbially in an occurrence (a noun with a preposition qualifying the predicate, as 'in the counsel of the wicked') is a qualifier there, not the verse's characteristic. The role is per occurrence: the same word may be the characteristic elsewhere.
In a simile, the predicates of the vehicle (the tree that yields, does not wither) are read for what they say of the one compared (the tenor), not as the vehicle's own acts.

An existing observation counts for a surface when its node names that occurrence (verse_lexical_id), or, with none, when the node's verse, Strong and surface match one occurrence only. A node that names a verse and no surface, or matches more than one occurrence, is set aside: it does not count for any surface.

When a verse is worked, every existing observation and node on it, of any stage, is checked against the verse by its wording. The stage is not an indication of the nature of an observation and is never used to filter. Each observation is accepted, modified (changed in place; the old value, the new value and the reason are kept in ib_observation_change), soft deleted (the `deleted` column, with the reason), merged (a duplicate description, into the observation that is kept) or, when its wording shows it is not verse understanding, left exactly as it is with the reason. The check's fixes are part of it and need no separate approval. Nothing is physically deleted.

A surface with no inner-being role in a verse has no observation of its own. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being has the role standalone, which is a role and not an absence; where it could be a qualifier it is read as the qualifier of the characteristic it serves.

The observations of a verse state what the verse shows, and Record enforces it from cfg_setting reading.observation_rules and reading.observation_items: an observation of a relevant surface carries parts.item (one of the nine items), is written as one of the kinds that item allows, on a basis the item allows (a read observation names its grounds), and carries what its item needs (polarity, mode, flag type; a party carries its route). The words that bear on an act are nodes of the observation of the act, never an observation of their own (bears_on_only_refused). Every surface with the role characteristic has each applicable item observed or stated absent with the reason; the verse always has an operation observation. A verse whose observations do not comply is not recorded (#2329).

For every surface with the role characteristic, the nine items of spec 4.2 (reading.observation_items) are each explored, and each applicable item is its own observation (parts.item), written once and applied to every characteristic it is true of by its nodes; a qualifier or shared observation carries nodes on every characteristic it covers. An item the verse does not show gets no observation and is stated absent on the surface (items_absent) with the reason; the meaning item is never absent. The operation item carries a mode (done, foreseen, commanded, negated, reported) and an action description of who or what does what, read from before and after as the verse itself states them (passage-level before and after are the claims process's); the verse always has an operation observation. A read observation (basis read) names its grounds in the words of the verse (parts.grounds). No observation restates the verse text (no run of more than reading.observation_items max_verse_words_copied words). The same text for all items is not an exploration of them. Which word is the characteristic is the verse's decision, never the cluster's (RG-03). The nuance pointers (reading.nuance_pointers) say where each nuance is recorded (#2329).

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Every older live observation with a live node on an occurrence of the row (a stage that is not the build's own) is answered in fill.older when the row is recorded, once: keep or restate (each with its marker), merge into a named observation, consume (live observations carry its meaning, stated in words, verified before it is deleted), delete as neither (comment first), or defer to a named collection (marked now; only the finding is left to that collection). An observation already marked by the validation, answered in a build or deferred is not asked again. A new observation whose text equals that of another live observation of the collection is refused, the other named. LayerCheck re-derives both from the tables. The end state of a collection's build is that every observation of its scope is marked and fixed or deleted, every word node complete or with its reason, and each deferral owned by a named collection.

A lookup of related data in the build or the validation is by an indexed column and takes a chunk of ids (cfg_setting layer.scan chunk); none runs once for each item of a list, and a statement that uses more work than layer.scan max_vm_ops is stopped and named, nothing written (lib/scanguard.py). The tests refuse a statement of the build whose query plan scans a table (layer.scan scan_ok lists the temporary tables a statement may scan).

rows.group: supposing, or holding something to be so
rows.asks: What do the stage 3 observations of this subgroup (its definition, its Strong's enrichment, its pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, relations and double meanings, with the stage 1 senses) show of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being: what is done and its mode, whether a refusal or a pursuit, what it is directed at, the outward act, the other party with the route, the circumstance, the chain of operations, and the dimensions of the working (what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives it, from the lexical variation the stage 3 observations record)? Each finding is one observation that rests on named observations (a traced node on each) and carries nodes on the occurrences those observations cover, with the role each has; an occurrence outside them is allowed only with a read-back (the verse and why). Every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared not used, with the reason. A finding is a building block and never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (stage 5).

interventions: Work from the observations: the stage 3 observations of the subgroup are the input, and the verses are base data read back only where an observation does not settle the point; a read-back is recorded (the verse and why).
Read the lexical variation (the different Strong's codes of a surface, the forms of a word, the double meanings) as the dimensions of how the working happens, not as a difference to be smoothed away.
A behaviour is discovered from the elements, not assumed from the subgroup: a subgroup may form one behaviour, part of one, join others, or form none.

Record building blocks only. A statement of what a behaviour is, is a claim and belongs to stage 5; stage 5 receives the observations and not the subgroups, so everything it will need from them is recorded here.
Check the original where an observation depends on the word's range (RG-08); do not force a meaning and never close on 'not X' (RG-10).

A word whose role is not its collection's is reclassified by the collection change procedure and the step reopens (B:129, B:134); a discovery outside the observations is recorded as a flag finding of type discovery and is not resolved inline (RW-07).

may_rest_on_besides.text: In 1Cor 8:2 the particle G1161 stands in the unit of the verb imagines; it is a small connective that carries no sense of supposing and the sense is carried by the verb of the same unit.

In 1Cor 8:2 the verb is the supposing of a person that he knows something, stated as a conceit that the verse corrects: the one who imagines he knows does not yet know as he ought. It is a held opinion of oneself that outruns the facts.

In 1Ti 6:5 the participle is the supposing of those depraved in mind that godliness is a means of gain; it is a belief held about what pays, joined in the verse to the loss of the truth, and it is a view that the verse condemns.
In Rom 2:3 the particle G1161 stands in the unit of suppose and carries the question that follows; it is a connective in the unit and the supposing is carried by the verb of the same unit.

In Jam 4:5 the verb is the readers' supposing that the Scripture speaks to no purpose; it is a conclusion about what Scripture means, put as a question that expects the answer no, in the context of friendship with the world.

In Joh 21:25 the verb is the writer's judgment that the world could not hold the books that would be written, an estimate made at the close; in Jam 1:7 it is the double-minded man's expectation that he will receive from the Lord, which the verse forbids. In the first it is a considered estimate, in the second an expectation held against the verse's warning.

In Luk 7:43 the verb is Simon's answer to Jesus, an estimate offered with a hesitant I suppose, and in Act 2:15 the crowd's wrong supposing that the apostles are drunk, which Peter corrects from the hour; in both it is a conclusion drawn by the speakers about what they see.
In Act 13:25 the verb is Paul's report of what John asked the people about their supposing of who he was; it is the people's opinion of John, which he corrects by saying he is not the one.

In Gen 18:28, 18:29, 18:30, 18:31 and 18:32 the word is Abraham's putting of a case to the Lord, supposing that so many righteous may be found; it is a hypothesis laid before God with each step down in number, not an opinion held.

In 2Sa 13:32 and 13:33 the verb is the king's supposing, which Jonadab warns him not to hold, that all the king's sons are dead; it is a conclusion drawn from a report and wrongly held, and the verses set it against what is true.

In Joh 11:31 the participle is the Jews' supposing that Mary goes to the tomb to weep; in Joh 20:15 Mary's supposing that the one speaking is the gardener; in Act 27:13 the sailors' supposing that they have gained their purpose; in each it is a conclusion drawn from what is seen, in the first two wrong or partial and in the last made before the wind changes.

In Luk 2:44 the participle is the parents' supposing that Jesus was in the group, in Act 14:19 the crowd's supposing that Paul is dead, and in Act 16:27 the jailer's supposing that the prisoners have escaped; in each it is a conclusion drawn from what is seen that the verse then shows to be wrong or to act on.

In Rom 1:21 the noun is the reasonings of those who knew God and did not honour him, which became futile; it names the thinking of persons as a thing that can fail, joined in the verse to the darkening of their foolish hearts.
In 2Cor 12:19 the verb is the readers' thinking all along that Paul has been defending himself to them; it is an assumption about his purpose that he corrects in the verse.

In 1Pe 4:1 the noun is the way of thinking, the purpose or mind that the readers are to arm themselves with, the same as Christ's in suffering; it is a settled attitude of mind and is commanded as a weapon.
In Rom 1:21 the word G2532 is the connective in the unit of thinking that joins the thinking to the darkened heart; it carries no sense of supposing and is a small word in the unit.

In Heb 11:15 the verb is the patriarchs' thinking of the land they had left, a remembering that would have given them the chance to return; it is a calling to mind and is set against the desire for a better country.
In Phili 1:17 the participle is the thinking of those who preach Christ from rivalry, that they raise up affliction for Paul; it is a purpose they hold, stated by Paul from outside as their intent.
In 1Cor 14:20 the noun is the thinking of the brothers, which is not to be a child's in evil but is to be mature; it names the faculty of the mind in the way it is used and is commanded to grow.

In Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, 2Ch 32:1, Neh 6:9 and Psa 64:5 the verb is a saying in the heart introducing a thought that follows in quotation: Jacob's fear of Esau, David's fear of reports to Gath, Achish's trust in David, the Jebusites' boast, the king's fear of the Syrians' ruse, Sennacherib's plan, the enemies' aim to frighten, and the plotters' question; in each the transl

In Luk 8:18, 1Cor 3:18, 10:12, 14:37, Gal 6:3, Phili 3:4 and Jam 1:26 the verb is the opinion of a person about himself: he thinks he has, he is wise, he stands, he is a prophet, he is something, he has reason for confidence, he is religious. In each the verse sets the opinion against the fact or the warning that follows, so it is a self-estimate that the verse tests.

In Rom 14:14 the participle is the one who reckons something to be unclean, for whom it is unclean; it is a conviction held about a thing that makes it unclean to him, with Paul's own conviction stated against it.

In 1Cor 7:36 the verb is a man's judgment that he is acting improperly toward his betrothed, a verdict on his own conduct that the verse puts under a condition and then resolves by what he is to do; it is an opinion of himself held under that condition.
In 1Sa 20:3 the verb is David's saying in his heart to Jonathan, the thought that Saul knows of their friendship and will keep it from him; the word is the inner speech that introduces the thought.

In 2Pe 1:13 the particle G1161 stands in the unit of think and joins the clause of the reminder to what precedes it; it carries no sense of thinking and the sense is carried by the verb of the same unit.

In the twenty verses G1380 is a mixture of opinion and question, the verb of what a person holds or is asked to hold. As a question to the hearer: what do you think (Mat 17:25, 18:12, 21:28, 22:17, 22:42, Joh 11:56), do you think (Mat 26:53, Luk 10:36, 12:51, 13:2, 13:4, Heb 10:29) and do not think (Joh 5:45), where Jesus asks or forbids an opinion. As a held view: the Gentiles who think they are
In Mat 9:4 the verb is the scribes' evil thinking in their hearts that Jesus knows, put as his question why they think it; it is an inner reasoning that is hidden from them but known to him.
In 2Pe 1:13 the verb is Peter's judging it right to stir up his readers by a reminder while he is in the body; it is a considered decision, with the reason given.

In 2Cor 12:6 the verb is Paul's wish that no one reckon more of him than what they see or hear, and in Phili 4:8 it is the command to think on whatever is true, honourable, just and pure; in the first it is the estimate others make of a person, in the second an act of dwelling the mind on what is good.
In Eph 3:20 the verb is what we ask or think, as the limit that God's working exceeds; it is the mind's conceiving of the possible, taken as a measure that God goes beyond.

In Mat 5:17 and 10:34 the verb is Jesus' forbidding of the supposing that he came to abolish the law or to bring peace; in Act 17:29 it is the supposing that the divine is like gold or stone; in 1Cor 7:26 it is Paul's judgment about the present distress. In the first three the supposing is a wrong opinion forbidden, in the last a considered judgment offered.

In Rom 12:3 the verb is the command not to think of oneself more highly than one ought, and in Phili 3:15 the maturity of thinking this way, with God to reveal any other; it is the mind's set or measure, as an estimate of oneself and a shared mind.

In 2Ki 18:20, Isa 36:5, 2Ch 13:8 and Eze 11:5 the verb is a saying that introduces what the speaker or the listeners hold or purpose: the Rabshakeh's challenge whether words are strategy, Abijah's charge that Israel thinks to withstand the kingdom, and the Lord's word that they speak in the city; in each it is the inner or spoken thought that the verse then answers.
In Est 4:13 the verb is Esther's not imagining to herself that she will escape in the king's palace; it is the thought she is told to put away.
In Psa 119:52 the verb is the psalmist's calling to mind of the Lord's rules of old, from which he takes comfort; it is remembering, not supposing.
In Isa 10:7 the verb is the king of Assyria's heart that does not think so, the intention that the Lord does not use as the king means; it is the planning of his heart set against the Lord's purpose.

In Job 6:26 and 35:2 the verb is a question put to Job, whether he thinks he can reprove words or that this is just; in Job 41:32 it is the likeness the deep seems to have; in Psa 119:59 it is the psalmist's turning to his ways, after which his feet turn to the testimonies; in Psa 144:3 it is the Lord's thought of man; in Jer 23:27 it is the false prophets' planning to make the people forget the n
In Dan 7:25 the verb is the little horn's thinking to change the times and the law; it is a purpose or intention of the one who speaks against the Most High, put in the Aramaic of the vision.

In Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3 and Jer 40:5 the word is the eye as the seat of judgment: the daughters may marry whom they think best, the princes ask whether Hanun thinks David honours his father, and the captain gives Jeremiah leave to go where it seems right; in each the translated think is the good in the eyes of the person, a judgment of what is fitting.
In 2Sa 18:27 the verb is the watchman's judgment, as he looks, that the running of the first is like Ahimaaz's; it is an estimate made from what he sees.
In Luk 12:17 the verb is the rich man's thinking to himself what he shall do, a reasoning within that is given in his own words; it is an inner deliberation about his crops.

In Mar 6:49, Luk 24:37, Joh 11:13, Joh 13:29 and Act 12:9 the verb is a wrong conclusion drawn from what is seen or heard: the disciples think they see a ghost, they think they see a spirit, they think Jesus spoke of sleep, they think Judas is sent to buy, Peter thinks he sees a vision. In each the verse says or shows that the conclusion is mistaken.
In 2Cor 9:5 and Phili 2:25 the verb is Paul's judging it necessary to send the brothers and Epaphroditus; it is a considered decision, with the reason following in the verse.
In Act 26:8 the verb is the judgment whether it is thought incredible that God raises the dead; it is an estimate put to the hearers as a question and answered by the speaker.

In Luk 12:17 the verb G3004G is the saying that introduces the rich man's thought to himself; the translated thought is carried by the verb of saying and the sense of reasoning is carried by the other verb of the same unit.

In 1Ti 3:7 the noun is the good testimony or repute that an overseer must have from outsiders; the translated well thought of is a reputation held by others, an account made of a person by those outside.

In 2Cor 10:5 the noun is the thought that Paul takes captive to obey Christ; it is the mind's content that is brought under Christ, in the verse set beside arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God.

In Mat 20:10 the verb is the first workers' expectation that they would receive more, and in Act 8:20 it is Simon's supposing that he could obtain God's gift with money; in the first it is an expectation that the master's answer corrects, in the second a wrong supposition that Peter rebukes.

In 1Cor 13:11 the verb is the child's thinking, set beside speaking and reasoning as one of the ways of a child that is put away with maturity; it is the mind's working at a stage, here to be outgrown.

In Jon 1:6 the word H0194 is the captain's perhaps, in the wish that the God may give thought to them; the translated thought is carried by the other word of the verse and the particle is the hope of the clause.

In Gen 20:11, 26:9, 31:31, 32:20, Exo 2:14, Jos 22:28, Jdg 3:24, 15:2, Rut 4:4, 1Sa 16:6, 18:11, 18:17, 18:21, 20:26, 2Sa 14:15, 14:17, 21:16, 2Ki 5:11, 20:19, Job 29:18, Psa 94:18, Isa 39:8, Jer 3:7, 3:19 and Eze 20:32 the verb of saying is the introduction of a thought held or said, rendered I thought or he thought. It is inner speech or spoken reasoning, quoted in each verse: Abraham's judgment

In Pro 14:15 and 21:29 the verb is the prudent man's giving thought to his steps and the upright man's to his way; it is a considering of one's own course before going on, in contrast with the simple who believes everything and the wicked who puts on a bold face.

In Deu 15:9 the noun is the unworthy thing in the heart, the thought that the seventh year is near so that one withholds from the poor; it is a matter that arises in the heart and then comes out as a saying, and it is warned against.

In Num 33:56 the verb is the Lord's purpose to do to the people what he had planned for the nations; in Psa 48:9 it is the people's dwelling on his steadfast love in the temple; in Psa 50:21 it is the wicked man's wrong supposing that God is like himself. The senses are a plan, a quiet dwelling and a false supposition.

In Deu 15:9 the word H1961 is the verb to be in the clause that warns against a base thought arising in the heart; it carries no sense of thinking and the sense is carried by the noun of the same verse.
In Lam 1:9 the verb is the failure to remember the end, said of Jerusalem that took no thought of her future; it is a calling to mind, wanting in the verse and given as the cause of her fall.

In 1Sa 18:25 the verb is Saul's design, the king's plan to put David at risk by a bride-price of foreskins; in Psa 40:17 it is the Lord's taking thought for the poor and needy speaker. The first is a plot, the second a gracious care.

In Gen 38:15 the verb is Judah's judgment that the veiled woman is a prostitute, an estimate drawn from her covered face that the story shows to be wrong; in Psa 73:16 it is the psalmist's trying to understand the prosperity of the wicked, which he finds wearisome until he enters the sanctuary. The first is a conclusion drawn from what is seen and the second an effort of understanding.
In Ecc 9:10 the noun is the reckoning or account that is not found in Sheol, listed with work and knowledge and wisdom; it names the mind's working as something that ends in the grave.
In 1Ch 28:9 the noun is the thought of every plan that the Lord understands, in David's charge to Solomon; it is the inner device of the mind as it is open to God.

In 2Sa 3:19 the word is the eye of the people, the seat of what seemed good, in Abner's report to David of all that seemed good to Israel; the translated thought is a reckoning of what was good, a judgment of the whole people.
In Jon 1:6 the verb is the captain's wish that the God may give thought to them, a Hithpael of the lexicon's to think; it is the hope that God may attend and save.

In Job 12:5 the noun is the thought of one at ease, which holds contempt for misfortune; it is a cast of mind of the comfortable toward the failing, and is quoted as Job's complaint against his friends.

In Mic 2:8 the verb is the reversal of what the people do to those passing by; the translated thought is not a thought but a turning back, carried by the verb of the clause, and names no act of the mind.
In Amo 4:13 the noun is man's thought which the Lord declares, said of the one who forms the mountains and the wind; it is the content of the mind as known to God.

tree.text: a conjunctive particle, marking the superaddition of a clause, whether in opposition or in continuation, to what has preceded, and it may be variously rendered but, on the other hand, and, also, now, etc.; καὶ δέ, when there is a special superaddition in continuation, too, yea, etc. It sometimes is found at the commencement of the apodosis of a sentence, Acts 11:17. It serves also to mark the resumption of an interrupted discourse, 2Cor. 2:10; Gal. 2:6

δέ,
but: adversative and copulative Particle,
__I answering to μέν (which see), τὴν νῦν μὲν Βοιωτίαν, πρότερον δὲ Καδμηίδα γῆν καλουμένην [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II without preceding μέν,
__II.1 adversative, expressing distinct opposition, αἰεί τοι τὰ κάκ᾽ ἐστὶ φίλα.. μαντεύεσθαι, ἐσθλὸν δ᾽ οὔτε τί πω εἶπας[Refs 5th c.BC+]; so in Prose, οὐκ ἐπὶ κακῷ, ἐλευθερώσει δέ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.2 copulative,
__II.2.a in explanatory clauses, ξυνέβησαν.. τὰ μακρὰ τείχη ἑλεῖν (ἦν δὲ σταδίων μάλιστα ὀκτώ) [Refs 8th c.BC+]: when a substantive is followed by words in apposition, Ἀρισταγόρῃ τῷ Μιλησίῳ, δούλῳ δὲ ἡμετέρῳ [Refs 5th c.BC+]; so in answers, διπλᾶ λέγειν. —Answ. διπλᾶδ᾽ ὁρᾶν [Refs]
__II.2.b in enumerations or transitions, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; with repetition of a word in different relations, ὣς Ἀχιλεὺς θάμβησεν.., θάμβησαν δὲ καὶ ἄλλοι [Refs 8th c.BC+]; in rhetorical outbursts, οὐκ ἂν εὐθέως εἴποιεν· τὸν δὲ βάσκανον, τὸν δὲ ὄλεθρον, τοῦτον δὲ ὑβρίζειν,—ἀναπνεῖν δέ. [Refs 4th c.BC+]; in a climax, πᾶν γύναιον καὶ παιδίον καὶ θηρίον δέ nay even beast, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; in the combination καὶ δέ [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.2.c answering to τε (which see), ἃ τῶν τε ἀποβαινόντων ἕνεκα ἄξια κεκτῆσθαι, πολὺ δὲ μᾶλλον αὐτὰ αὑτῶν [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.3 implying causal connexion, less direct than γάρ, [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.4 in questions, with implied opposition, ἑόρακας δ᾽, ἔφη, τὴν γυναῖκ; [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.4.b τί δ; what then? to mark a transition in dialogue; see at {τίς}.
__II in apodosi:
__II.1 after hypothetical clauses, εἰ δέ κε μὴ δώωσιν, ἐγὼ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι if they will not give it, then I.., [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.1.b after temporal or relative clauses, with ἐπεί, ἕως, etc., [Refs 8th c.BC+]; with demonstrative Pronouns or adverbs answering to a preceding relative, οἵηπερ φύλλων γενεή, τοίη δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν [Refs 8th c.BC+]: sometimes after a participle, οἰόμενοι.. τιμῆς τεύξεσθαι, ἀντὶ δὲ τούτων οὐδ᾽ ὅμοιοι.. ἐσόμεθα [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.2 to resume after an interruption or parenthesis, χρόνου δὲ ἐπιγινομένου καὶ κατεστραμμένων σχεδὸν πάντων..,—κατεστραμμένων δὲ τούτων.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; with an anacoluthon, ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ ἄρα,—οἷ ἂν θεὸς θέλῃ.. τῇ ἐμῇ ψυχῇ ἰτέον, αὕτη δὲ δή.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.3 to begin a story, ἦμος δ᾽ ἠέλιος.. well, when the sun.., [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.4 to introduce a proof, τεκμήριον δέ, σημεῖον δέ, (see entry).
__B POSITION of δέ. It usually stands second: hence frequently between Article and substantive or preposition and case; but also after substantive, or words forming a connected notion, hence it may stand third, γυναῖκα πιστὴν δ᾽ ἐν δόμοις εὕροι [Refs 5th c.BC+]; so in Prose after a negative, οὐχ ὑπ᾽ ἐραστοῦ δέ, to avoid confusion between οὐ δέ and οὐδέ, [Refs 5th c.BC+]

__I.2 with adverbs, εὖ φρονεῖν think rightly, περί τινος [Refs 5th c.BC+]; to be sane (compare infr. IV), [Refs 5th c.BC+] also, to be well disposed, see below [Refs]; κακῶς, καλῶς φ., [Refs 8th c.BC+]; μῶρα, πλάγια φ., [Refs 5th c.BC+]

__II.2 frequently with neuter adjective,
__II.2.a φ. τινί τινα to have certain thoughts for or towards any one, to be so and so minded towards him, πατρὶ φίλα φρονέων kindly minded towards him, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; φρονεῖς εὖ τοῖς ἠγγελμένοις you rejoice at them, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τοιαῦτα περί τινος φ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]: to be minded so and so, think or purpose such and such things, ἀγαθὰ φ. [Refs 8th c.BC+]; φίλα φ.[Refs 8th c.BC+]; κρυπτάδια φ. to have secret purposes, [Refs]; ἀταλὰ φ. to be gaily disposed,[Refs 8th c.BC+]; πυκινὰ φ. have wise thoughts, be cunningly minded, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; ἐφημέρια φ. think only of the passing day,[Refs 8th c.BC+]; τυραννικὰ φ. to have tyranny in mind, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ἀρχαιϊκὰ φ. to have old-fashioned notions, [Refs]; τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς φ., [NT]; also οὐ παρδάλιος τόσσον μένος ὅσσον Πάνθου υἷες φρονέουσιν the panther's courage is not so great as is the spirit of the sons of Panthus, [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.2.b especially frequently in the phrase μέγα φρονεῖν to be high-minded, have high thoughts, to be high-spirited, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; of lions and boars, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; in Attic dialect, frequently in bad sense, to be presumptuous, ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτῷ, ἑαυτοῖς μέγα φ., [Refs 5th c.BC+]; φ. ἐφ᾽ αὑτῷ τηλικοῦτον ἡλίκον εἰκός.. [Refs 4th c.BC+] to have over-high thoughts, [Refs 5th c.BC+] (but simply, pluck up courage, ἐπὶ τῷ γεγενημένῳ [Refs 5th c.BC+]: rarely in plural, μείζω τῆς δίκης φ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; with superlative, οἱ μέγιστον φρονοῦντες [Refs 5th c.BC+]; take pride in, ἐπὶ παιδεύσει μέγα φρονοῦντες [Refs 5th c.BC+]; μέγα φ. ὅτι.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; μέγα φ. μὴ ὑπείξειν haughty in their resolution not to.., [Refs 5th c.BC+] alone, ={μέγα φ., φρονήσας ἐφ᾽ αὑτῷ} [Refs 2nd c.AD+] to be poor-spirited, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ἧσσον, ἔλασσον φ. τινος, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.2.c of those who agree in opinion, τά τινος φρονεῖν to be of another's mind, be on his side or of his party, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; also ἶσον ἐμοὶ φρονέουσα thinking like me, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; τὠυτὸ or κατὰ τὠυτὸ φ. to be like -minded, make common cuase, [Refs 5th c.BC+] think differently, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; ἄλλῃ φ. think another way, [Refs]

findings.text: A thought is said within oneself and given as quoted speech in twenty-eight verses: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Saul, David, Naaman, Hezekiah and others each think something and the verse gives it. The code behind most is the verb 'to say', whose lexicon sense includes saying in one's heart; in several the thought is spoken to another in a dialogue.

A supposition is held about another person or a state of affairs and acted on, and in the verses of the Gospels and Acts it proves mistaken or unverified: Mary supposed to be going to the tomb, the gardener, the group on the journey, Paul dead, the prisoners escaped, a ghost, a spirit, a sleep, a purchase, a vision. In each the verb of thinking states the supposition and the verse then states what the people did or found.

A person holds a view of himself, which the verse then tests: that he is wise (1Cor 3:18), something (Gal 6:3), religious (Jam 1:26), a prophet (1Cor 14:37), standing (1Cor 10:12), with grounds for confidence (Phili 3:4), and that he knows (1Cor 8:2). The verb states a self-estimate, and the verse sets it beside deceiving oneself, folly or knowledge.

A thought is held as a purpose or plan in Num 33:56, 1Sa 18:25, 2Sa 21:16, 2Ch 13:8, 2Ch 32:1, Isa 10:7, Jer 23:27, Dan 7:25, Rut 4:4 and Phili 1:17: the Lord's purpose, Saul's snare, a giant's killing, withstanding a kingdom, conquering cities, destroying nations, making the people forget, changing the times, telling a kinsman and afflicting Paul. The verb is the same as for a supposition, and the verse gives the purpose within two words of it in several.

A view is asked of the hearer in eight verses, where Jesus or the writer puts the question and the hearer's opinion is what is sought: what do you think, Simon (Mat 17:25), a man with a hundred sheep (Mat 18:12), a man with two sons (Mat 21:28), is it lawful (Mat 22:17), what of the Christ (Mat 22:42), which of the three (Luk 10:36), the feast (Joh 11:56) and how much worse a punishment (Heb 10:29). The direction of the asking runs from the speaker to the hearer.

The supposition is forbidden, denied or withheld in twelve verses: do not think (Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Joh 5:45), we ought not to think (Act 17:29), that person must not suppose (Jam 1:7), let no one think me foolish (2Cor 11:16), let not my lord suppose (2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33), not to think too highly (Rom 12:3, twice), do not think to yourself (Est 4:13), the heart does not so think (Isa 10:7) and no thought of her future (Lam 1:9). In each the negator reaches the member itself, one to seven words from it.

In these verses the act is a refusal as the grammar states it: Jesus rules out the supposition that he came to abolish the Law or bring peace, accuse you, or that God is like an image; Paul rules out thinking too highly of oneself and asks that no one think him foolish. The refusal is of a supposition about Jesus, about God or about oneself, and is spoken by Jesus, by Paul and by the one counselling.

Where the supposition is held and acted on the act is a pursuit of its content: the people follow Mary out, go a day's journey, stone Paul, draw the sword, sail on, send a gift, give a daughter to a snare. The thought is the ground of a move toward the thing supposed.

What is held to be so is dying or perishing in Gen 26:9, Job 29:18 and Jon 1:6 (the dying stands 2 words after the member and is the content of the thought), escaping in Gen 32:8, Est 4:13, Act 16:27 and Rom 2:3 (the escape is within ten words and is part of what is supposed), and someone's being dead in 2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33 and Act 14:19.

What is held to be so is peace and security in 2Ki 20:19 and Isa 39:8 (Hezekiah's thought, security 3 to 4 words after) and in Mat 10:34 and Luk 12:51 (the supposition that Jesus came to bring peace, which is corrected); and fortified cities in 2Ch 32:1 and a guard in Jer 40:5. The same word peace is held by Hezekiah and denied of Jesus' coming.

What is held to be so is a state of the one who holds it: wise (1Cor 3:18, the wise within 2 words), religious (Jam 1:26), something when he is nothing (Gal 6:3), a prophet (1Cor 14:37), standing (1Cor 10:12), knowing (1Cor 8:2), with reason for confidence (Phili 3:4, confidence 6 before and 1 after) and thinking highly of oneself (Rom 12:3, faith 6 after). In each the object of the thinking is the thinker.

What is held to be so is another person's state or act: a prostitute (Gen 38:15, her face covered 2 words after), a gardener (Joh 20:15), in the group (Luk 2:44), drunk (Act 2:15), dead (Act 14:19), a sleep (Joh 11:13), a ghost (Mar 6:49), unclean (Rom 14:14, the uncleanness 2 words before) and not clean (1Sa 20:26). The object is a person or a thing in a state the speaker has not verified.

What is thought of is the steadfast love of the Lord in Psa 48:9 (1 word after the member), and what answers the thought of falling is the same steadfast love in Psa 94:18 (3 words after); the poor are the ones the Lord thinks of in Psa 40:17 (poor 3 before, needy 2 before) and the ones the unworthy thought turns from in Deu 15:9 (poor 10 after). The thinking is directed at the Lord's love or at the poor.

The outward act that follows a supposition is stated in the same verse: the Jews follow Mary (Joh 11:31, going 2 words after), Joseph's people go a day's journey (Luk 2:44), the crowds stone Paul (Act 14:19), the jailer draws his sword (Act 16:27, killing 2 words before), the sailors weigh anchor (Act 27:13), Saul gives his daughter as a snare (1Sa 18:21, give 1 after), and Jacob sends a present (Gen 32:20, present 3 after). The supposition and the act it leads to stand in the one sentence.

A supposition issues in a spoken answer or a question in the exchanges of Gen 18:29 to 18:32, Gen 31:31, Exo 2:14, Est 4:13, Luk 7:43 and Luk 13:2: the supposition is put in the speaker's own words as part of a dialogue, with 'answered' 1 to 13 words from the member.

Fear stands within three words before the thought in Gen 31:31, Exo 2:14, 2Sa 14:15 and Neh 6:9, in Luk 24:37 (startled and frightened, 3 and 1 words before) and in Gen 20:11 (the fear of God, 3 words after). In five of the six the fear is named before the thought and the thought comes from it.

Anger, hiding and hunger stand beside the thought in Gen 18:30 and Gen 18:32 (the Lord's anger), 2Ki 5:11 (Naaman's anger, 4 words before), Psa 64:5 (secretly, 1 word before), 2Ki 7:12 (hide, 2 words before; hungry, 6 before) and Gen 38:15 (the covering of her face, 2 words after). The thought arises in a person who is angry, hiding or hungry, or who is faced with something concealed.

Affliction, suffering and crying stand with the thought in Lam 1:9 (affliction), 1Cor 7:26 (the present distress, 3 words after), Phili 1:17 (afflict, 1 after), 1Pe 4:1 (Christ suffered, within 2 words), Luk 13:2 (suffered), Mar 6:49 (cried out, 4 after), Joh 11:31 and Joh 20:15 (weeping) and Deu 15:9 (the cry to the Lord, 14 after). The thinking is set in verses of distress or of a response to it.

The heart or the mind is named with the thought in Deu 15:9 and 2Sa 13:33 (1 word), Isa 10:7 (2 words), Eze 20:32 and Rom 1:21 (3 words), 1Ch 28:9, Mat 9:4 and 1Ti 6:5 (4 words), Eze 11:5 (6) and Jam 1:26 (10). The verses place the thought in the heart or mind of the one who holds it.

Knowing stands with the thought in thirteen verses: in 1Cor 8:2 knowledge is 1 word after the member and is what the person thinks he has, in Ecc 9:10 knowledge is 1 word after and is stated as absent in Sheol, in Mat 9:4 and Eze 11:5 the thinking is known by another, and in Act 12:9 and Rom 1:21 knowing is stated as lacking or as turned to futile thinking. The thought is set beside knowledge, held, lacking or known by another.

Trust, loyalty and silence stand with the thought in 1Sa 27:12 (Achish trusted David, 2 words before), 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5 (whom do you trust, 8 after), Mic 2:8 (trustingly, 1 before), Psa 48:9 and Psa 94:18 (steadfast love within 3 words) and Psa 50:21 (silence 1 word before the false supposition). Trust is the ground of Achish's thought, and the Lord's silence is the ground of the supposition that he is like the one who has done these things.

Asking and calling stand with the supposition in Mat 6:7 (those who pray suppose they will be heard), Mat 26:53 (the supposition whether Jesus cannot appeal), 2Sa 14:15 (the request the woman came to make), 2Ki 5:11 (Naaman supposes the prophet will call on the name of the Lord, 4 after), Jer 3:19 (call me Father, 1 after) and Jon 1:6 (call out to your god, 4 before the hope). The supposition is about being heard or about a call.

Searching and finding stand with the supposition in Gen 18:28 and Gen 18:30 ('find' is the condition of each supposed number), Mat 18:12, Luk 2:44 and Joh 20:15 (the search follows the supposition or the question) and Joh 5:39 (searching the Scriptures, 4 words before the supposition). The supposition is set in a verse of a search or of a condition to be found.

Sin, judging and evil stand with the supposition in Luk 13:2 (worse sinners), Eze 18:14 (a son who sees his father's sins), Rom 2:3 (you who judge), Joh 5:45 (accuse), Mat 9:4 (evil, 1 word after), Psa 64:5 (evil, 5 before), 1Cor 14:20 (evil, 2 before) and Pro 21:29 (the wicked, 5 before). In Mat 9:4 the evil is what is thought; in the others it stands in the clause of the person who thinks.

Believing, honor, reward and the commandment stand with the thought in Pro 14:15 (the simple believes, 3 words before), Rom 12:3 (faith, 6 after), Jam 1:26 (religion, 12 after), 2Sa 10:3 and 1Ch 19:3 (honoring, 4 after), 1Cor 12:23 (honor, 3 after), Heb 10:29 (punishment, 1 before), Mat 22:17 (pay, 2 after) and Num 36:6 and 1Cor 14:37 (the Lord's command). In each the thought is about something owed, believed or commanded.

Truth, righteousness and the lawful stand with the supposition in Job 35:2 (just, 2 after), Mat 22:17 (lawful, 1 after), 2Cor 12:6 (truth, 5 before), 1Ti 6:5 (truth, 1 before), Phili 4:8 (honorable and just, 13 to 15 before) and Gen 18:28 (the righteous in the case put). The thought is a judgment whether something is right, true or lawful.

War, return and the endurance of a held position stand with the thought in 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5 (war, 5 after), 1Sa 18:17 (fight and battles), Mic 2:8 (war, 1 after), Jer 3:7 (return, 5 after, expected and not done), Heb 11:15 (return, 8 after, what thinking of the land would have allowed), 2Ch 13:8 (withstand, 1 after) and 1Cor 7:26 (remain, 9 after). The thought is of conflict, of return or of holding out.

Small words stand in the units of the surfaces of this group and do not carry the sense of supposing: the connective G1161 in 1Cor 8:2, Rom 2:3 and 2Pe 1:13, G2532 in Rom 1:21, the particles and pronouns H3588A (Gen 20:11), H1931 (Pro 21:29), H0834A (Eze 20:32), H0853 (Neh 6:9), the preposition H0413 (Jer 40:4), the copula H1961 (Deu 15:9) and the returning H7725G (Mic 2:8). They are read in their verses as standalone and were read at stage 1 for what they do.

In the verses of the quoted thought the partner collections hold words that are not words of their collection's meaning: the surface 'surely' stands as a member of 'hear' in Exo 2:14, Jdg 3:24, 1Sa 16:6, 1Sa 20:26 and 2Ki 5:11; 'unworthy' as a member of 'reward' in Deu 15:9; 'presence' and 'present' as members of 'offer' in Rut 4:4 and 1Cor 7:26; and 'will' as a member of 'desire' in 2Sa 14:17 and 2Ki 7:12. These are recorded as open item #2536 and are not resolved here.
